worldBackground:
This is My Hero Academia's Japan, following the canon anime, with two changes: every character is their canon age plus three, and every U.A. student lives on campus from the first day. Never state numeric ages; call people first-years, young adults, veterans or small children. The canon children Eri and Kota stay small children and are always written as children.

About four in five people have a Quirk, registered in early childhood: an Emitter that projects outward, a Transformation that changes the body for a while, or a Mutant body that never switches off. Every Quirk has a scope, a limit and a cost the body shows. Heteromorph people face prejudice, and people with no Quirk face pity and bullying. Public Quirk use without a hero license is illegal except in self-defense and supervised training; even a rescue brings a police statement and possibly a reprimand, and vigilantes and villains risk arrest. The Hero Public Safety Commission writes the rules, issues and revokes licenses and manages how the public sees heroes. Licensed heroes work through agencies, take sidekicks and interns, sell merchandise and climb the Hero Billboard Chart JP; at the start of the year All Might is Number One, Endeavor Number Two and Hawks Number Three. The prefectural police investigate, take statements and make arrests, and rely on heroes in Quirk fights. Tartarus holds the worst offenders.

U.A. Academy is Japan's national hero academy above Musutafu: a three-year residential program for high-school graduates, run by Principal Nezu with a faculty of working pro heroes. Call it U.A. Academy, or U.A. in dialogue, and nothing else. Its courses are the Hero Course (Classes 1-A and 1-B for first-years), General Studies, Support and Management, with homerooms, uniforms, class representatives, the entrance exam and the broadcast Sports Festival, the biggest sporting event in the country, where agencies scout talent. Every student lives in Heights Alliance from the first day: one building per Hero Course class, shared halls for the other courses, curfew, sign-out sheets and weekend visits home. Nobody commutes. Shiketsu Academy in the west is U.A.'s closest rival; other academies train heroes across the country.

The story opens right after move-in at Heights Alliance, at the start of the first year. All Might has just joined the faculty, and nobody has been attacked. The League of Villains is so new and small that almost no one has heard of it: Tomura Shigaraki, Kurogiri and thugs hired through brokers. Stain hunts the heroes he judges false. Brokers such as Giran sell jobs, hideouts and gear. The last yakuza houses, the Shie Hassaikai in Osaka the best known, survive as designated villain groups watched by the police. The Meta Liberation Army is history, remembered through an old manifesto with a quiet following.

Canon events are conditional pressures, not a script: the first-day Quirk test, the Battle Trial, the class representative vote, the media break-in, the USJ attack, the Sports Festival and everything after happen only when their causes are in place, with their real actors and capabilities, and the player can change how they go; the changes stick. Nobody foresees them. NPC records are fixed and describe each person as they are now: build on them, never contradict them, and never treat a later event as already past.

Tone: shonen heroics, heroic, funny and dangerous in turn. Rivalry, comedy and friendship sit beside real danger; Quirks have visible costs; heroes save people first. School exercises are supervised and nonlethal, with teachers who stop a bout before lethal harm; a genuine villain attack is an emergency, not a match. Quiet days between crises are part of the story.

Daily life is ordinary modern Japan with Quirks in it. The school and business year starts in April under the last cherry blossoms; Golden Week brings a run of holidays in early May, the rainy season fills June, and summer break begins late in July. People pay in yen or by phone, ride packed commuter trains and the shinkansen, buy dinner at convenience stores open all night, follow hero news on phone apps and station screens, and queue, bow and apologize as a matter of course. Musutafu lies in Shizuoka on Suruga Bay, 45 minutes from Tokyo by shinkansen; Osaka and Fukuoka are hours away by train, and nobody crosses the country in an afternoon without a reason. People use family names with polite distance and move to first names only with friends and family, so the change gets noticed. A phone camera is always nearby: a Quirk caught on video can be online within the hour, and one rescue or one mistake can make a stranger famous by evening.
questGenerationGuidance:
Generate a quest only when a concrete objective and a plausible way to discover and accept it exist. The world offers its own authored quests for the canon class beats and events (the first-day Quirk test, All Might's battle trial, the class representative vote, hero names, internships, exams, the license exam and the rest); never generate a quest that repeats one of them or a canon event, under any title. Generated quests fill the time around them. A lecture, a lunch, a sparring session or an evening in Heights Alliance need not become a quest. An offer is not acceptance, a promised reward is not a paid one, and an unaccepted opportunity never becomes a failed quest. Each quest states plainly what happens and who runs it, what changes on success or failure, who or what actually stands in the way, and what is concretely gained; it never grants before completion what only the story can grant (a license, a ranking, a transfer, a bond). Rewards follow agreed terms: a shift earns its pay, and a defeated opponent creates no purse.

Quest families by Path:
- Hero Course (Class 1-A or 1-B): training-ground exercises, rescue drills, Quirk control work, rival rematches, costume and support gear requests, class duties, Sports Festival preparation, then internships, the provisional license and agency work as the story reaches them.
- General Studies, Support Course, Management Course: a transfer ambition proven in public events, workshop commissions and gear testing with Power Loader, agency publicity and branding, event logistics, ranking analysis, and the Sports Festival as a showcase.
- U.A. Faculty: lesson and exam design, student welfare and discipline, dorm and campus security, staff meetings with Principal Nezu, hero work outside class, mentoring a struggling student.
- Licensed Sidekick: patrols, arrests, rescues, reports, agency rivalries and the hero whose name is on the door.
- League of Villains Recruit: tests of loyalty, scouting, recruitment through brokers, logistics for an operation and Shigaraki's moods; refusal and betrayal have consequences.
- Independent Villain: the player's own goals: jobs through brokers, territory, debts, rivals, fences and police heat; never automatic League membership.
- Vigilante: night patrols, small rescues the law ignores, informants, and police and hero pressure; every save risks arrest.
- Civilian Life: a job, rent, neighbors and regulars, a street closed by a villain attack, a family member in trouble, a favor that grows.

Stakes scale to the stage. At the start trouble is local: a grade, a rivalry, a street crime, a debt, a reprimand. Pros, faculty, police and Commission staff outclass a new player, who succeeds against them through evasion, delay, negotiation or cleverness. Villains bring their real capabilities; a Nomu or a League lieutenant is a threat, never filler. Opposition comes from canon-consistent actors: canon characters by their exact names in roles their records support, or generated people of ordinary standing who never stand in for a canon character.

Canon events are conditional pressure. Build quests around an arc only when play reaches its causes, give the player real ways to change the outcome, and keep its consequences. No quest resolves a canon arc off-screen, no quest giver foreshadows an event as certain, and hidden truths surface only through discovery or earned confession.

Ordinary-life quests fill the time between crises: a part-time shift, a study group before an exam, a gear repair, a weekend visit home, a club event, a favor for a classmate, a lost pet, a dorm dispute, a train delay that strands someone across the city. After a major incident the next quests lean toward aftermath, recovery, inquiries, press and ordinary life before a new crisis builds from its own causes. A quiet success can conclude completely; not every problem hides a conspiracy.

Party quests: every member keeps their own objectives, grades, scores and choices; shared work never pools results into automatic success, and one member's answer never pledges the others.

Failure keeps its real consequence: a failed exam means remedial lessons or a poor grade, a botched rescue means an inquiry, an exposed criminal job means heat. Never a generic death, fine or permanent enemy. If the player leaves or delays, the situation moves on its own causes. Access, licensing, schedules, curfew, competence and consent set the conditions; obstacles are real, never padding. Meaningful player help counts even if someone else finishes; work done without the player is not player success. Completed objectives, injuries, reprimands, press and changed relationships persist. School contests, lessons and exams stay supervised and nonlethal, while genuine villain attacks remain real emergencies.
